newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany's IG Chemie keeps 1997 wage demand open.
newsitem.headline: Germany's IG Chemie keeps 1997 wage demand open.

text.p: Regional leaders of Germany's IG Chemie trade union on Wednesday declined to specify a 1997 pay demand for chemical workers in a bid to open up forthcoming negotiations with employers.
But they confirmed they would still demand that chemical firms back away from a controversial new law cutting sick pay entitlements when the two sides hold talks later this month.

Rainer Kumlehn, head of IG Chemie in the state of Hesse, said the union wanted to discuss the 1997 wage rise together with demands for job protection measures and further investment in trainee positions.

But he said that while any wage agreement would have to take into account overall inflation and productivity increases in the chemical sector, the regional union commission "did not want to burden the pay round with a concrete wage demand".
Kumlehn added the decision of the Hesse wage commission was intended as a recommendation to other regional union leaders, who will soon be deciding their 1997 wage demands.

The VCI (Verband der Chemischen Industrie) chemical industry employers group said it would not be making a comment on the union's position before national talks between the two sides start on November 19.
Workers and employers in the chemical sector have traditionally been able to find agreement on annual wage levels more easily than in other German industries.
But relations between the two have this year been soured by earlier attempts by firms such as BASF AG to impose a new law cutting sick pay from 100 percent of salary to 80 percent.
Some 13,000 BASF workers protested last month when it announced plans, since postponed, to implement the law.
